title: A Postcards for the Interior
premise: Paloma Galloway, a translator whose childhood language survives only in fragments they can no longer speak fluently, hears an unrecorded lullaby on a late-night radio broadcast — a song their late grandmother composed and swore never to share. The broadcast traces to a community radio station in the old neighborhood slated for demolition and rerouting, where someone is archiving the voices of a disappearing immigrant enclave. Returning home, Paloma uncovers that their mother gave the song away decades ago to protect a family secret: the grandmother's real history of collaboration, exile, and an unacknowledged first family. As Paloma translates a box of unsent postcards written in a language they are forgetting, they must choose between the loyalty that kept the family's story buried and the truth that might finally let them belong — to the neighborhood, to the language, and to themselves. In the end, Paloma records the song in their own imperfect voice, postcards mailed at last, as the last bus makes its final rerouted run.
about_author: Kestrel Amberdale is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between two languages and now writes about the ones that get away. They live near a decommissioned bus depot and collect unsent letters at estate sales.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. We meet them mid-career as a translator who deflects intimacy with practiced ease, losing words from their grandmother's language weekly. A client dinner ends with Paloma alone, mouthing a lullaby they can only half remember. Emotional beat: the quiet grief of assimilation and the armor of invisibility.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Half-asleep, the radio plays the lullaby — complete, orchestrated, credited to no one. Paloma confirms with their stunned mother that it was composed by grandmother Ida and never shared. The mother's fear is immediate and disproportionate. Emotional beat: the first crack in the family's sealed story.

chapters.title: The Last Route to Marrow Street
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. They trace the broadcast to a community station in the old neighborhood, where a young archivist, Dev, is recording elders before the district is rezoned and the bus line rerouted. Paloma arrives under the pretense of a translation job. Emotional beat: homecoming as trespass; the neighborhood remembers them better than they remember it.

chapters.title: Postcards Without Addresses
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In Ida's abandoned flat, Paloma finds a shoebox of unsent postcards in the fading language, addressed to someone named only 'T.' Translation is slow and humiliating — they must ask Dev for help, surrendering their armor of competence. Emotional beat: vulnerability as the price of reentry.

chapters.title: What the Mother Kept
chapters.summary: Mother's POV, in flashback and present. We learn she gave Ida's song to a musician friend during a family crisis, trading her mother's privacy for protection from a truth about Ida's wartime years and a first family left behind. Emotional beat: loyalty as a burden inherited without consent.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Ear
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev has noticed the song's melody appearing in three separate elder interviews — a shared memory the community never spoke aloud. They press Paloma gently, sensing a story the archive needs. Paloma lies, badly. Emotional beat: the seduction and danger of being truly seen.

chapters.title: T.
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The postcards resolve: T. was Ida's first daughter, left behind in the old country, presumed lost. The final postcard, dated the year of Ida's silence, says the song was written for her. Paloma realizes the radio version carries an extra verse only T. would know — someone answered it. Emotional beat: the ground gives way.

chapters.title: Rerouting
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Confrontation with the mother detonates the family: the song was given away to keep T.'s existence from reaching Ida's dying ears — or so the mother claims. Paloma accuses her of choosing silence over truth; the mother accuses Paloma of loving a dead woman more than the living. Paloma walks out. Emotional beat: the climax of loyalty versus truth, both sides wounded and half-right.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Paloma and Dev. Dev finds the second voice in the archive: an elderly woman, Ruth — T.'s daughter — recorded months ago, singing the answering verse, believing no one would ever connect it. Paloma and Ruth meet in the station as demolition notices go up. Emotional beat: grief met with kinship; the lost family found on the far side of the secret.

chapters.title: Broadcast in a Borrowed Voice
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the station's final broadcast before closure, Paloma sings the lullaby — imperfect, accent thickening where the language returns — and reads the last postcard aloud, addressed at last. The mother arrives unannounced and stays. The last rerouted bus passes the station as the song ends. Emotional beat: belonging not as inheritance received, but as truth finally spoken and shared.
